The clavichord is a European stringed keyboard instrument, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-4-8, in use from the late Middle Ages to the Classical period. In a rectangular case, brass or iron strings run sideways, and small metal tangents at the back of the keys strike the strings and stay in contact, sending the vibration through the bridge to the soundboard. The player can change the volume by the force of the key, and the pressure of the tangent produces tiny changes of pitch. Because it is so quiet, it was used mainly for practice at home, as an aid to composing, for solos or small-scale accompaniment, and in a pedal version for organists to practise on.
古鍵琴為弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 314.122-4-8: The clavichord is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-4-8; its sounding body is a set of strings stretched sideways, which the source records as usually brass, or brass combined with iron; the strings are in pairs and pass over a curved wooden bridge. The end of each key lever carries a brass tangent, which strikes the string and stays in contact while the key is held. The damping is a strip of cloth woven in among the strings. The material of the case is generally not stated; only the instrument Mozart used is recorded as walnut, and the other parts are not given.
古鍵琴為歐洲弦鳴樂器，霍恩博斯特爾-薩克斯分類法編號314.122-4-8。發聲: The clavichord is a European chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122-4-8. Sound comes from a metal tangent at the end of the key striking a brass or iron string; while the key is held the tangent stays on the string, starting the vibration and defining the sounding length, so both pitch and volume depend on the touch. The player can change the volume by pressing harder or more lightly, and use the pressure of the tangent to make a clavichord vibrato; when the key is released a strip of cloth damps the string. The range was mostly four octaves early on and up to six later. The volume is very low, which suits small rooms and practice; unlike the piano, the hammer rebounds after the strike, and unlike the harpsichord it does not pluck.
古鍵琴約十四世紀出現，最早明確記載為1404年德語詩《Der Minne Reg: The clavichord appears about the fourteenth century; the earliest clear record is a German poem of 1404, Der Minne Regel. It was common in German-speaking lands, Scandinavia and the Iberian peninsula from the sixteenth to the eighteenth century, and an English royal expense record mentions it in 1502; Matteo Ricci took one to Beijing in 1601. Before the 1730s most were small instruments of four octaves; later ones reached six. It declined around 1850; in the 1890s Arnold Dolmetsch revived its making and Violet Gordon-Woodhouse promoted its playing; in the twentieth century it gave rise to the electric Clavinet.
古鍵琴音量極低，歷史上多用於家庭練習、作曲輔助、小型房間中的鍵盤獨奏與伴奏，風琴: The clavichord is very quiet; historically it was used for practice at home, as an aid to composing, for keyboard solos and accompaniment in small rooms, and organists practised on the pedal version. Today it is played by lovers of Renaissance, Baroque and Classical music, and has entered other genres: the electric Clavinet is often linked with funk and disco rock, and Stevie Wonder used it on 'Superstition' and 'Higher Ground'; Guy Sigsworth, Björk, Tori Amos and Keith Jarrett have also used it.
坐姿端正，手指彎曲輕放鍵上。擊弦古鋼琴透過金屬片擊弦發聲，觸鍵力度可細微控制音量: Sit upright with the fingers curved and resting lightly on the keys. The clavichord sounds by metal tangents striking the strings, and the force of the touch gives fine control of volume. Practising the vibrato (Bebung) is the characteristic technique: after pressing a key, add a little more pressure and then release it, which makes a wavering sound.
